title: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
summary: Why read plus write copies every byte twice, and how Linux avoids it: sendfile from the page cache, splice and tee over pipe page references, MSG_ZEROCOPY with completion notifications, and when it pays.
outcomes: Explain where the CPU copies happen in a read and write loop, and which ones each zero-copy call removes
Write a correct sendfile loop that handles short transfers, EAGAIN, the 0x7ffff000 cap and a header via TCP_CORK
Use splice and tee with pipes to forward data between sockets, and compute the calls needed for a given pipe size
Implement MSG_ZEROCOPY send and error-queue reaping with inclusive id ranges, and know when a deferred copy happens
Decide from message size and data path whether zero-copy beats copying, using measured numbers

lessons.title: Where the copies go in a read and write loop

blocks.md:
A static file server, a Kafka broker and a video CDN all do the same thing millions of times a day: take bytes that sit in a file and push them out of a socket. The obvious code is a loop of `read(file, buf, n)` then `write(sock, buf, n)`. It works, and it is correct. The problem is what it costs.

Recall from the system calls course that every `read` and `write` crosses from user mode into the kernel and back, and that the kernel keeps recently used file data in the **page cache**, a pool of kernel memory holding file pages. Let us follow one chunk of the file through that loop.

blocks.title: One chunk through read() then write()

scenes.caption: The chunk starts on disk. The disk controller copies it into the page cache by DMA (direct memory access: the device writes memory without the CPU). If the page was already cached, this step is skipped.
read() makes the CPU copy the bytes from the page cache into your buffer. The data does not change; it is just duplicated across the user/kernel boundary.
write() makes the CPU copy the same bytes back into kernel memory, this time into the socket's send buffer. Your program never looked at them.
Finally the network card pulls the data out of the socket buffer by DMA and puts it on the wire.
Totals per chunk: 4 copies (2 by DMA, 2 by the CPU) and 2 system calls, so 4 user/kernel mode switches. The 2 CPU copies are pure overhead: the bytes leave exactly as they arrived.

blocks.md: This is exactly how the [Kafka design document](https://kafka.apache.org/42/design/design/) describes the common file-to-socket path: four copies and two system calls. **Zero-copy I/O** is the family of techniques that removes the CPU copies (the DMA copies are unavoidable, a device has to move the bytes). Nothing is literally copied zero times; the name means *zero copies by the CPU between kernel and user memory*.

Why care? A CPU copy costs cycles and memory bandwidth on every byte, and it evicts useful data from the CPU caches. Willem de Bruijn's MSG_ZEROCOPY paper profiled a netperf process streaming TCP with 1 MB writes and found **79%** of its cycles inside `copy_user_generic_string`, the kernel's user-to-kernel copy routine. When the program does almost nothing but move data, copying *is* the program.

The syscall count grows too. Sending a 1 MiB file with a 64 KiB buffer takes 16 reads and 16 writes, plus one final read that returns 0 at end of file: 33 system calls and 2 MiB of CPU copying to ship 1 MiB.

blocks.prompt: You already know mmap from the prerequisite course. If you `mmap` the file and call `write(sock, mapped_ptr, len)`, how many CPU copies remain per chunk?
blocks.reveal:
**One.** mmap maps the page cache pages straight into your address space, so the copy into a user buffer disappears. But `write` still copies from those pages into the socket buffer, because the socket API takes a user pointer and must assume you may change that memory right after the call returns.

mmap also brings its own costs: page faults on first touch, and a SIGBUS if another process truncates the file while you are sending it.

blocks.title: CPU copies and mode switches per chunk

scenes.caption: CPU copies of each byte. sendfile keeps data inside the kernel, and on a NIC that supports scatter-gather and checksum offload even the copy into the socket buffer disappears (lesson 2 explains why).
User/kernel mode switches per chunk (2 per system call). Simplified: mmap + write can add page-fault entries into the kernel, and sendfile can move many chunks in one call.
DMA copies are the same everywhere: one from disk into the page cache (skipped on a cache hit) and one from memory to the NIC. Zero-copy never removes these.

blocks.md: Zero-copy means removing the **CPU copies between the page cache, user memory and socket buffers**. Device DMA still happens. The win scales with bytes moved, so it matters when a program mostly shovels data it does not inspect.

Zero-copy does not mean faster for every request. It removes per-byte work but adds per-call and per-page bookkeeping. For small messages the copy is cheap and the bookkeeping can cost more, as lesson 5 measures.

blocks.question: A server reads each file with read() into a 64 KiB buffer, then write()s it to a TCP socket. Hot files are always in the page cache. Which costs does the read/write loop add that an in-kernel transfer would avoid?
options: The DMA from disk into the page cache
Two CPU copies per byte and two system calls per chunk
The DMA from the socket buffer to the NIC
Nothing: the page cache already makes it zero-copy
blocks.explain: With hot files there is no disk DMA at all, and the NIC DMA is needed by every method. What the loop adds is the copy page cache to user buffer, the copy user buffer to socket buffer, and a read plus a write per chunk. The page cache avoids disk reads, not memory copies.

blocks.question: How many CPU copies per byte does mmap + write leave, and why not zero?
options: Zero, because the mapped pages are the page cache
Two, because mmap copies the file into anonymous memory
One, because write() must copy from the user pointer into the socket buffer
One, because mmap copies the file on the first page fault
blocks.explain: mmap removes the page cache to user copy: the mapping points at page cache pages. But write() is a copying interface. Once it returns you may modify the buffer, so the kernel copies the bytes into the socket buffer during the call.

lessons.title: sendfile: from the page cache straight to the socket

blocks.md: `sendfile(out_fd, in_fd, offset, count)` asks the kernel to move `count` bytes from `in_fd` to `out_fd` itself. Because the copy happens inside the kernel, the [sendfile(2) man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/sendfile.2.html) says it is more efficient than `read` plus `write`, which would move data to and from user space. Your process never gets a pointer to the bytes, so the kernel never has to protect against you changing them mid-flight.

The rules, from the man page:

- `in_fd` must support mmap-like operations, so it is typically a regular file. It **cannot be a socket**. (Since Linux 5.12, if `out_fd` is a pipe, sendfile is turned into a splice and splice's rules apply.)
- `out_fd` can be any file since Linux 2.6.33; before that it had to be a socket.
- If `offset` is not NULL, reading starts there, `*offset` is advanced, and the file's own offset is left alone. This lets many connections share one open file.
- One call transfers at most 0x7ffff000 bytes (2,147,479,552), and like `write` it may transfer fewer than asked.

blocks.title: What sendfile does inside the kernel

scenes.caption: Your process makes one call and passes two file descriptors, not a buffer. Nothing is copied into user memory.
If the pages are not cached yet, they are read from disk into the page cache by DMA, exactly as for read().
Instead of copying, the kernel builds packet buffers whose payload fragments point at the page cache pages, and takes a reference on each page so it cannot be evicted mid-send.
A scatter-gather NIC assembles each packet itself: headers from the kernel buffer, payload straight from page cache memory. The CPU never touches the payload bytes.
Simplified: if the NIC cannot scatter-gather or compute checksums, the kernel must read the payload anyway, so it makes a private copy. That is the one remaining CPU copy in the bars of lesson 1.

blocks.md: Two hardware features make the CPU copy disappear. **Scatter-gather DMA** lets the NIC build one packet from several memory pieces, so kernel-made headers and page cache payload need not be contiguous. **Checksum offload** lets the NIC compute the TCP checksum, so the CPU never has to read the payload. de Bruijn's paper describes this sendfile path: page cache fragments are linked into the packet's fragment array, with a reference on each page, and are replaced by private copies wherever the payload must be read, such as software checksumming.

Inside Linux, sendfile is built on the splice machinery you will meet in lesson 3: `do_sendfile` in `fs/read_write.c` calls `do_splice_direct`, which uses an internal pipe to hold page references between the file and the socket.

blocks.title: A sendfile loop on a 3 GiB file

scenes.caption: Start: offset 0, 3 GiB (3,221,225,472 bytes) to send on a blocking socket.
The first call asks for all 3 GiB but the kernel caps one transfer at 0x7ffff000 bytes, so it returns 2,147,479,552.
The short return is not an error. The loop subtracts what was sent; 1,073,745,920 bytes remain. The kernel advanced pos for us.
Second call sends the rest. Two calls move 3 GiB with no user-space copy at all.

On a non-blocking socket, a full send buffer gives EAGAIN: wait for writability with epoll and retry. EINVAL or ENOSYS means sendfile cannot handle these descriptors, and the man page suggests falling back to read and write.

blocks.md: Real responses need a header in front of the file. If you `write` the HTTP header and then `sendfile` the body, TCP may send the small header in its own packet. The man page recommends **TCP_CORK** ([tcp(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/tcp.7.html)): while it is set, TCP holds partial frames, and clearing it flushes them, with a 200 ms ceiling after which corked data goes out anyway.

blocks.caption: Header and file body in full packets. nginx's tcp_nopush directive turns on TCP_CORK on Linux when sendfile is used.

blocks.md: Production servers use exactly this. nginx has `sendfile on;` (off by default), `tcp_nopush` for corking, and `sendfile_max_chunk`, which defaults to 2m because, in nginx's words, without a limit one fast connection may seize the worker process entirely ([nginx core module docs](https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_core_module.html)). Kafka stores its log on disk in the same binary format consumers read, so the broker can sendfile log chunks straight from the page cache; when consumers are caught up, the docs note, the disks may see no reads at all.

sendfile shares page cache pages with the network stack. The man page warns that the transferred part of the file must stay unmodified until the reader on the other end has consumed it. If another process rewrites the file mid-send, the bytes on the wire can be a mix of old and new.

sendfile cannot encrypt. Kafka's docs say sendfile is not used when SSL is enabled, because TLS runs in user space. Kernel TLS (kTLS) changes this: with the TLS key installed on the socket, the kernel encrypts sendfile data into TLS records of at most 2^14 bytes. Encryption reads every byte, so it is no longer copy-free unless the NIC does the crypto.

blocks.question: Your proxy receives bytes on one TCP socket and forwards them to another. A teammate suggests `sendfile(out_sock, in_sock, NULL, n)`. What happens?
options: It works and is zero-copy end to end
It fails, because in_fd must support mmap-like operations and a socket does not
It works but copies through user space
It fails, because out_fd may not be a socket
blocks.explain: sendfile reads from something with page-cache-like pages, a regular file. A socket is not that, so the call fails with EINVAL. Forwarding between sockets needs splice with a pipe in the middle (lesson 3). out_fd being a socket is the classic use case, so the last option is wrong.

blocks.question: sendfile(sock, fd, &pos, 3221225472) on a blocking socket returns 2147479552. What should the code do?
options: Treat it as an error and close the connection
Reset pos to 0 and retry the whole file
Switch to read and write for the rest of the file
Call sendfile again with the remaining 1073745920 bytes; pos was already advanced
blocks.explain: A short count is normal: one call moves at most 0x7ffff000 bytes, and a socket can also accept less. Because a non-NULL offset pointer is updated by the kernel, the loop just calls again with what is left.

lessons.title: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references

blocks.md:
sendfile covers file to socket. What about socket to socket (a proxy), or tapping a stream to two places? Linux's general tool is a trio of calls built around the **pipe**. From the [splice(2) man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/splice.2.html):

- `splice(fd_in, off_in, fd_out, off_out, size, flags)` moves data between two descriptors **where at least one is a pipe**, without copying between kernel and user address space.
- `tee(fd_in, fd_out, size, flags)` duplicates data from one pipe into another without consuming it.
- `vmsplice(fd, iov, nr_segs, flags)` maps ranges of user memory into a pipe.

The trick is what a pipe is inside the kernel. The man page explains that a pipe buffer is a set of **reference-counted pointers to pages**. To "copy" a page into another buffer, the kernel creates a new pointer to the same page and increments its reference count. Only pointers move, not page contents. A pipe has a fixed number of slots: the default capacity is 16 pages, 65,536 bytes with 4 KiB pages ([pipe(7)](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/pipe.7.html)).

blocks.title: Six file pages through splice and tee

scenes.caption: A 24 KiB file region sits in the page cache as 6 pages, A to F. Both pipes are empty: 16 slots each (simplified: real refcounts also count other holders).
splice(file, pipe1, 24576): six slot pointers now refer to the page cache pages, and each page's count goes up. No byte of A to F was copied.
tee(pipe1, pipe2, 24576): pipe 2 gets its own pointers to the same pages. Pipe 1 is not consumed, so the data can now go two places.
splice(pipe1, sock): the socket takes over pipe 1's page references for its packets and pipe 1 empties. Counts stay 3 until the network stack frees those packets.
The peer ACKs and TCP frees the packets: counts drop to 2. Pipe 2 still holds the data for its second consumer, for example a log file.

blocks.md:
A zero-copy TCP proxy uses a pipe as the middle stage:

1. `splice(client_sock, NULL, pipe_w, NULL, 65536, SPLICE_F_MOVE | SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK)` pulls received data into the pipe.
2. `splice(pipe_r, NULL, server_sock, NULL, n, SPLICE_F_MOVE | SPLICE_F_MORE)` pushes it out.

Every transfer is two system calls, and each round is bounded by the pipe capacity. Moving 1 MiB through a default 64 KiB pipe takes 16 rounds, so 32 splice calls, with zero bytes copied into user space. HAProxy offers exactly this as `option splice-auto`, and its docs warn that each spliced connection needs spare pipes and that early kernels had buggy implementations (2.6.29 is the first it calls properly working).

The flags are mostly hints:

- `SPLICE_F_MOVE` asks to move pages instead of copying. Its first implementation was buggy, so since Linux 2.6.21 it is a no-op that is still accepted.
- `SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK` makes the pipe side non-blocking; the other descriptor can still block unless it is `O_NONBLOCK`. This is what you want inside an epoll loop.
- `SPLICE_F_MORE` tells a socket more data follows, like `MSG_MORE`.
- `SPLICE_F_GIFT` (vmsplice only) gives your pages to the kernel; you may never modify them again.

blocks.prompt: vmsplice puts *your own* memory into a pipe without copying. Then you splice the pipe to a socket and reuse the buffer for the next message. What can go wrong?
blocks.reveal: The socket may still be holding references to your pages when you overwrite them, so **the new bytes can go out on the wire** in place of the old ones, including in TCP retransmissions. vmsplice gives no notification of when the kernel is done with the pages. de Bruijn's paper notes that programs worked around this by polling the socket's queue size (SIOCOUTQ), which is imprecise: an empty send queue does not mean the data has left the machine. This gap is exactly what MSG_ZEROCOPY (lesson 4) fills.

blocks.md: One more relative: `copy_file_range(fd_in, off_in, fd_out, off_out, size, 0)` copies between two regular files inside the kernel. Its [man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/copy_file_range.2.html) notes it lets filesystems use **reflinks** (two files sharing the same copy-on-write disk blocks) or server-side copy on NFS, so a "copy" may not move data at all. Since Linux 5.19, cross-filesystem copies work only if both filesystems are the same type and support it; otherwise it fails with EXDEV.

Pipes are the kernel's zero-copy buffer: slots of reference-counted page pointers. splice moves those pointers between a pipe and any descriptor, tee duplicates them, and sendfile itself runs on this machinery with a hidden internal pipe.

blocks.question: A proxy splices 1 MiB from one socket to another through a pipe with the default capacity. Each splice moves a full pipe's worth. How many splice calls does it make?
blocks.explain: Default capacity is 16 pages, 65,536 bytes. 1,048,576 / 65,536 = 16 rounds, and each round is one splice into the pipe and one out of it: 32 calls. Two would need a 1 MiB pipe (settable with F_SETPIPE_SZ); 256 is the number of 4 KiB pages.

blocks.question: Which call fails with EINVAL?
options: splice(file_fd, &off, pipe_w, NULL, n, 0)
splice(sock_fd, NULL, pipe_w, NULL, n, SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK)
tee(pipe1_r, pipe2_w, n, 0)
splice(file_fd, &off, sock_fd, NULL, n, 0)
blocks.explain: splice requires that at least one side is a pipe; file to socket has none, so it returns EINVAL. For file to socket use sendfile, which builds the internal pipe for you. The other three each involve a pipe on the correct side.

lessons.title: MSG_ZEROCOPY: sending from your own memory safely

blocks.md:
sendfile only helps when the data is already in a file. Most servers build responses in memory: an RPC reply, a compressed block, a tensor. For those, `send(sock, buf, len, 0)` has to copy, and the reason is a promise in the API: when `send` returns, you may immediately overwrite `buf`. The kernel can only keep that promise by taking its own copy.

**MSG_ZEROCOPY**, added by Willem de Bruijn at Google and described in the [kernel documentation](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/msg_zerocopy.html), changes the promise. The kernel **pins** your pages (locks them in memory so they cannot be moved or swapped out), links them into packets just as sendfile links page cache pages, and tells you later when you may reuse them.

Three pieces make it work:

1. **Opt in per socket**: `setsockopt(fd, SOL_SOCKET, SO_ZEROCOPY, &one, sizeof one)`. The kernel ignores unknown send flags, so a legacy program might already pass the flag by accident; the socket option shows real intent.
2. **Flag per call**: `send(fd, buf, len, MSG_ZEROCOPY)`. Mixing flagged and unflagged sends on one socket is allowed.
3. **Completion notifications** on the socket's **error queue**, read with `recvmsg(fd, &msg, MSG_ERRQUEUE)`. Each socket keeps a 32-bit counter. Every flagged send that sends data takes the next id, starting at 0. Failed and zero-length sends take no id. The counter counts calls, not bytes.

blocks.title: Three zero-copy sends and their completion

scenes.caption: Opt in once per socket. Without SO_ZEROCOPY, the MSG_ZEROCOPY flag would simply be ignored.
Each send pins the buffer's pages and returns at once. The kernel assigns ids 0, 1 and 2 in call order. The app must not touch those buffers yet.
The NIC DMAs the payload directly out of the app's pages. TCP keeps the packets for possible retransmission until the peer acknowledges them.
When the last packet referencing ids 0 to 2 is freed, the kernel queues a notification. Consecutive ids merge into one range while unread.
The app reads the error queue without blocking and recycles all three buffers in one step.

blocks.md: A notification is a `sock_extended_err` with `ee_origin = SO_EE_ORIGIN_ZEROCOPY`, `ee_errno = 0`, and an **inclusive range** `[ee_info, ee_data]` of completed ids. The zero errno is deliberate: a normal pending socket error would block other operations until read, and these must not. Errors are always signalled, so poll reports POLLERR (and epoll EPOLLERR) without you asking for it; the docs recommend reading without blocking every few sends rather than waiting after each one.

blocks.title: Ids, pinned buffers and coalesced ranges

scenes.caption: Six MSG_ZEROCOPY sends have returned. Ids 0 to 5 are all pinned: their memory belongs to the network stack for now.
Packets for ids 0 to 3 are acknowledged and freed. TCP completes in order, so 4 completions merge into one queued notification: [0, 3].
The app reads [0, 3] and reuses those 4 buffers. The queue is now empty.
Id 4 completes: a new notification [4, 4]. Then id 5 completes before the app reads; the kernel sees 5 = 4 + 1 and extends it to [4, 5] instead of queueing another.

blocks.title: Reaping completions

scenes.caption: The error queue holds one notification. Reads from it never block.
It is a zero-copy notification with range 0 to 3: four sends completed.
ee_code does not have ZEROCOPY_COPIED set, so the kernel really sent from our pages.
Release ids 0, 1, 2 and 3. The loop uses id != hi + 1 so it still terminates when the 32-bit counter wraps.
The next recvmsg fails with EAGAIN: nothing pending, so return to the event loop.

blocks.md:
Passing MSG_ZEROCOPY is a **hint**, not a guarantee. The kernel may still copy deeper in the stack, for example when the device cannot scatter-gather, when a checksum must be computed in software, or when IPsec must encrypt the payload. It still sends a notification, and sets `SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED` in `ee_code`. Such a deferred copy can cost more than copying during the call, because the data is no longer warm in cache, so the docs suggest a process may stop passing the flag on that socket.

Packets looped back to a local socket **always** take a deferred copy, because a local receiver that never reads would otherwise keep your pages pinned forever. Benchmarks over loopback therefore show no improvement.

A notification means "the kernel has released your pages", **not** "the data was delivered". With a deferred copy it can arrive before the copied data is even transmitted. Never use it as a transmit or delivery acknowledgement.

Writing into a buffer before its id completes does not crash anything, but it corrupts your own stream: the modified bytes may go out on the wire or in a retransmission. The kernel docs: kernel integrity is not affected, but a buggy program can corrupt its own data stream.

Pinned memory is limited. A send fails with `ENOBUFS` when the socket exceeds its option-memory limit or the user exceeds the locked-pages limit (`ulimit -l`). The kernel also caps how many bytes one completion record can cover: `msg_zerocopy_realloc` in `net/core/skbuff.c` stops merging sends into one record past 512 KiB (`1 << 19`), after the paper observed a case where 75 calls merged into one record and the first buffer's completion was delayed far too long.

blocks.question: A program sends with MSG_ZEROCOPY and gets notification [7, 9] with SO_EE_CODE_ZEROCOPY_COPIED set. What does it know?
options: Sends 7, 8 and 9 were delivered to the peer
Buffers for sends 7, 8 and 9 may be reused, and the kernel ended up copying their data
Only send 9 completed; 7 and 8 are still pinned
Sends 7 to 9 failed and must be retried
blocks.explain: The range is inclusive, so ids 7, 8 and 9 are released. The COPIED code says the data went out via a copy, so zero-copy brought no benefit for them; it does not signal failure. Neither part means delivery: a notification is about page ownership, not about the peer.

blocks.question: An engineer benchmarks MSG_ZEROCOPY between two processes on one machine over 127.0.0.1 and sees no gain. Most likely reason?
options: MSG_ZEROCOPY only works for UDP
The SO_ZEROCOPY option resets on loopback
Packets looped to a local socket always incur a deferred copy
Loopback has no error queue
blocks.explain: The kernel converts zero-copy packets to private copies on paths that loop back to local sockets, to bound how long pages stay pinned. The docs warn that such a test will not show any improvement; benchmark between two hosts.

lessons.title: When zero-copy pays: measurements, limits and choices

blocks.md: Copy avoidance swaps a per-byte cost (copying) for per-call and per-page costs: pinning pages, building fragment lists, tracking references and processing notifications. Which side wins depends on message size. de Bruijn measured it with netperf streaming one 10 Gbps TCP flow at different send sizes, counting cycles with perf, with the process and the network interrupts on separate CPUs.

blocks.title: MSG_ZEROCOPY cycles as a percent of copying

scenes.caption: Cycles in the sending process, zero-copy divided by copy, computed from the paper's Mcycle table. At 1 MB sends the process does only 8% of the work: a 92% saving.

Cycles on both CPUs (process plus interrupt handling). The saving is smaller, 20% to 39%: the interrupt CPU's work does not shrink, and in the paper's table it even grows by 12% to 29% with zero-copy.

blocks.md: A simple model fits these numbers. If a send of $s$ KB costs $c\,s$ cycles to copy, and zero-copy costs a fixed $F$ per call plus $p\,s$ for the pages, the ratio is $r(s) = p/c + (F/c)/s$. A least-squares fit to the paper's 5 points (our fit, not the paper's) gives:

blocks.caption: Break-even is where r = 1: about 1.4 KB for process cycles and about 1.9 KB system-wide, in this microbenchmark. Both are extrapolated below the smallest measured size, 4 KB.

blocks.title: Fitted cost model: zero-copy versus copy

scenes.caption: System-wide fit with the paper's measured points. Below about 1.9 KB the zero-copy curve rises above 1: bookkeeping costs more than the copy it saves.
Process-only fit: the copy dominated, so the floor drops to 0.09. Points still show system-wide data.

A real application pays more per call (notification handling, keeping buffers alive). Quadrupling the fixed cost to 2.8 KB pushes break-even past 7 KB, consistent with the docs' rule of thumb of around 10 KB.

blocks.md: Simplified: a microbenchmark that only streams data is the best case. The [kernel docs](https://www.kernel.org/doc/html/latest/networking/msg_zerocopy.html) say MSG_ZEROCOPY is generally only effective for writes over around 10 KB. The paper's real workloads agree. An internal RPC benchmark *regressed* by 15% with 2-byte RPCs and improved by 23% with 98 KB RPCs. A mixed machine-learning workload ran 7.5% faster, a content delivery system gained 5% peak QPS, and a remote block device gained under 2%, which the paper attributes to it already hashing all data for integrity before sending.

Zero-copy pays when messages are large, the CPU is the bottleneck and the program does not touch the bytes. Any step that reads every byte (software checksums, encryption, hashing, compression) brings the copy back almost for free and erases most of the win.

The same ideas appear in newer interfaces:

- **io_uring zero-copy send** (`io_uring_prep_send_zc`, see the [liburing man page](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/io_uring_prep_send_zc.3.html)) usually posts **two** completions. The first carries the send result with `IORING_CQE_F_MORE`; the second, flagged `IORING_CQE_F_NOTIF`, says the buffer may be reused. With registered buffers the pinning is paid once, at registration.
- **io_uring zero-copy receive** ([kernel docs](https://docs.kernel.org/networking/iou-zcrx.html)) puts packet payloads straight into user memory. It needs NIC header/data split, flow steering and RSS (receive side scaling, which spreads flows across receive queues) so only chosen flows reach the zero-copy queue, while the kernel TCP stack still processes headers, unlike kernel bypass such as DPDK.
- **kTLS device offload** has a `TLS_TX_ZEROCOPY_RO` option that lets sendfile data go to the NIC without an in-kernel copy, if the file is not modified mid-send.

nodes.label:
MSG_ZEROCOPY or send_zc
if sends > ~10 KB

scenes.caption: Start from where the bytes already live. Each source has its own copy-free path.
Static files and log segments: sendfile from the page cache, corked so the header shares a packet with the body.
Proxies: splice socket to pipe to socket. sendfile cannot read from a socket.
Generated data: MSG_ZEROCOPY with notifications, or io_uring send_zc, for large sends only. Small sends, loopback traffic and software-checksummed paths are cheaper to just copy.

blocks.md: Common failure modes: modifying a buffer or file before the kernel is done with it (silent corruption on the wire), forgetting to drain the error queue (pinned memory grows until ENOBUFS), benchmarking over loopback (always copied), and assuming a notification means the peer received the data.

blocks.question: A service sends 200-byte RPC replies at high rate and spends 30% of CPU in copies. Should it switch to MSG_ZEROCOPY?
options: Yes, any copy removed is a pure win
Yes, but only over loopback
No, at 200 bytes per send the per-call pinning and notification costs exceed the copy; batch replies into larger sends first
No, MSG_ZEROCOPY only supports UDP
blocks.explain: Per-call cost dominates small sends: the paper saw a 15% regression with 2-byte RPCs, and the docs say it is generally only effective above about 10 KB. Coalescing many small replies into large writes attacks the overhead first; zero-copy can follow once sends are big.

blocks.question: Kafka serves fetches with sendfile. A cluster enables TLS between clients and brokers. What happens to the zero-copy path?
options: Kafka stops using sendfile, since TLS runs in user space and the bytes must be encrypted there
Nothing, sendfile encrypts automatically
sendfile switches to splice
The broker uses MSG_ZEROCOPY instead
blocks.explain: Kafka's design docs say sendfile is not used when SSL is enabled, because the TLS library lives in user space. Kernel TLS can restore an in-kernel path, but encryption still reads every byte unless a NIC offloads it.
